options.a: Average daily intake estimated to meet the needs of half (50%) of healthy individuals in a life-stage group
options.b: Average daily intake sufficient to meet nutrient needs of nearly all (97–98%) healthy individuals in a group
options.c: Highest average daily intake likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects for most healthy individuals
options.d: Observed average intake of apparently healthy people, used when evidence is insufficient to set a requirement

distractorExplanations.a: That defines the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR), which covers 50% of the group; the RDA is set above the EAR to cover 97–98%.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL), the ceiling for safe intake, not the RDA target for adequacy.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes the Adequate Intake (AI), used only when there is not enough evidence to calculate an EAR and therefore an RDA.

options.a: Urinary urea nitrogen exceeds dietary nitrogen intake
options.b: Protein intake nitrogen equals nitrogen losses
options.c: Nitrogen intake exceeds losses, as in pregnancy
options.d: Total energy intake equals resting energy expenditure

distractorExplanations.a: Losses greater than intake describe negative nitrogen balance (catabolism, stress, starvation), not equilibrium.
distractorExplanations.c: Intake greater than losses is positive nitrogen balance, seen in growth, pregnancy, and recovery, not equilibrium.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses energy balance with nitrogen balance; equilibrium is defined by nitrogen intake versus nitrogen output.

options.a: Adipose tissue and liver
options.b: Brain and skeletal muscle
options.c: Liver and skeletal muscle
options.d: Red blood cells and liver

distractorExplanations.a: Adipose tissue stores energy as triglyceride, not glycogen; only the liver half of this pair is a major glycogen store.
distractorExplanations.b: The brain holds only trace glycogen and depends on blood glucose; the liver, not the brain, is the second major store.
distractorExplanations.d: Red blood cells lack mitochondria and store no glycogen; they rely on circulating glucose via anaerobic glycolysis.

options.a: Carbohydrate grams per serving multiplied by the food's GI value
options.b: Blood glucose response relative to a reference carbohydrate
options.c: Insulin response relative to an equal-calorie reference food
options.d: Total carbohydrate and fiber content per 100 grams of food

distractorExplanations.a: That describes glycemic load (GI × available carbohydrate per serving ÷ 100), which builds on GI but is a different measure.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes the insulin index; GI is based on the blood glucose curve after 50 g of available carbohydrate.
distractorExplanations.d: GI is a measured physiological response, not a nutrient composition value read from the label or food database.

options.a: Alanine, glutamate, and other dispensable amino acids the liver synthesizes
options.b: Leucine, lysine, and other indispensable amino acids that must come from diet
options.c: Glutamine, arginine, and other conditionally indispensable amino acids
options.d: Glycine, serine, and other amino acids synthesized from glycolytic intermediates

distractorExplanations.a: Alanine and glutamate are dispensable: the body makes them by transamination, so they are not dietary essentials.
distractorExplanations.c: Conditionally indispensable amino acids become essential only in stress or illness; healthy adults can synthesize them.
distractorExplanations.d: Glycine and serine are made from 3-phosphoglycerate, so they are dispensable, not essential, amino acids.

options.a: Thiamin (TPP)
options.b: Niacin (NAD+)
options.c: Riboflavin (FAD)
options.d: Vitamin B6 (PLP)

distractorExplanations.a: Thiamin pyrophosphate drives oxidative decarboxylation (e.g., pyruvate dehydrogenase), not amino group transfer.
distractorExplanations.b: NAD+ from niacin is the electron carrier in dehydrogenase reactions; transaminases use PLP, not NAD+.
distractorExplanations.c: FAD from riboflavin carries electrons in oxidation reactions such as succinate dehydrogenase, not transamination.

options.a: Intake estimated to meet the requirement of half the healthy people in a group
options.b: Intake meeting the needs of 97–98% of healthy people in a life-stage group
options.c: Highest usual intake unlikely to pose risk of adverse effects for most people
options.d: Lowest intake at which adverse effects were observed in human or animal studies

distractorExplanations.a: That defines the EAR, the median requirement used to assess group adequacy, not the upper safety limit.
distractorExplanations.b: That defines the RDA, the adequacy goal for individuals; the UL marks the top of the safe range instead.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the LOAEL; the UL is set below the NOAEL/LOAEL by applying an uncertainty factor for safety.

options.a: It mainly adds stool bulk and speeds transit without affecting lipids
options.b: It lowers LDL by being absorbed and blocking hepatic cholesterol synthesis
options.c: It may help lower LDL cholesterol and blunt postprandial glucose
options.d: It raises postprandial glucose by speeding gastric emptying

distractorExplanations.a: That describes insoluble fiber such as wheat bran; soluble fiber forms viscous gels that do affect lipids and glucose.
distractorExplanations.b: Soluble fiber is not absorbed; it lowers LDL by binding bile acids in the gut, unlike statins that block synthesis.
distractorExplanations.d: Viscous soluble fiber slows gastric emptying and glucose absorption, so it blunts rather than raises the glucose peak.

options.a: Protein intake is high and amino acids are converted to glucose
options.b: Insulin levels are high and lipolysis in adipose tissue increases
options.c: Carbohydrate availability is very low and fat oxidation rises
options.d: Carbohydrate intake is high and excess glucose is converted to fat

distractorExplanations.a: Gluconeogenesis from amino acids supplies glucose and tends to restrain ketogenesis; it is not the driver of ketosis.
distractorExplanations.b: High insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis; ketones rise when insulin is low relative to glucagon.
distractorExplanations.d: Abundant carbohydrate drives lipogenesis and suppresses fatty acid oxidation, so ketone production falls.

rd-exam-readiness-check-principles-014.explanation: Ketone bodies are produced by the liver when carbohydrate availability is very low, leading to increased fat oxidation for energy, as seen in prolonged fasting or very low-carbohydrate diets. Typical settings are prolonged fasting and very low-carbohydrate (ketogenic) diets.

options.a: Assessment, nutrition diagnosis, intervention, monitoring/evaluation
options.b: Screening, assessment, intervention, monitoring/evaluation
options.c: Assessment, intervention, nutrition diagnosis, monitoring/evaluation
options.d: Nutrition diagnosis, assessment, intervention, monitoring/evaluation

distractorExplanations.b: Screening precedes the NCP and is not one of its four steps; this sequence also drops the nutrition diagnosis step.
distractorExplanations.c: Places intervention before diagnosis; the intervention must target the etiology identified in the nutrition diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.d: A nutrition diagnosis cannot be made before assessment data are collected; assessment is step 1 of the NCP.

options.a: Problem, Evaluation, Supporting data
options.b: Prognosis, Etiology, Severity
options.c: Problem, Etiology, Signs/Symptoms
options.d: Problem, Evidence, Strategy

distractorExplanations.a: Evaluation belongs to the monitoring/evaluation step; the E in PES is the etiology, or root cause, of the problem.
distractorExplanations.b: The P is the nutrition problem (diagnostic label), not a prognosis, and S stands for signs/symptoms, not severity.
distractorExplanations.d: Strategy belongs to the intervention step; PES ends with signs/symptoms, and the E is the etiology, not evidence.

options.a: A uniform 45% carbohydrate prescription for every patient with diabetes
options.b: Strict avoidance of sucrose, with sugar-free foods used at every meal
options.c: High-protein meals to replace carbohydrate and prevent hypoglycemia
options.d: Consistent carbohydrate intake pattern individualized to meds/activity

distractorExplanations.a: ADA Standards state there is no ideal macronutrient percentage; the carbohydrate plan is individualized.
distractorExplanations.b: Sucrose can fit within the carbohydrate plan when substituted for other carbohydrate; strict avoidance is not required.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein does not raise glucose reliably or treat hypoglycemia, and replacing carbohydrate with protein is not standard MNT.

options.a: Restricted to 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day to slow progression of residual kidney function
options.b: Higher than typical pre-dialysis needs to account for dialytic losses
options.c: Lowered to 0.3–0.4 g/kg/day with keto-acid analogs to limit urea buildup
options.d: Unchanged from pre-dialysis needs because dialysis replaces kidney function

distractorExplanations.a: Protein restriction is used in CKD stages 3–5 not on dialysis; hemodialysis patients need about 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day.
distractorExplanations.c: Very low-protein diets with keto-acid analogs apply to selected non-dialysis CKD patients, not hemodialysis.
distractorExplanations.d: Dialysis removes amino acids and increases catabolism, so needs rise above pre-dialysis levels rather than staying the same.

rd-exam-readiness-check-nutrition-care-0.explanation: Patients on hemodialysis typically require higher protein intake, around 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day, to compensate for amino acid and protein losses during dialysis sessions. This is generally higher than the protein restrictions often recommended for pre-dialysis chronic kidney disease. Targets are individualized.

options.a: Slowly refeeding a well-nourished patient after a 24-hour fast
options.b: Aggressively refeeding a severely malnourished patient
options.c: Rehydrating a well-nourished patient after acute vomiting
options.d: Giving a hypocaloric diet to a patient with obesity

distractorExplanations.a: A short fast in a well-nourished person does not deplete intracellular phosphate, potassium, or magnesium stores.
distractorExplanations.c: Fluid replacement without prior starvation does not trigger the insulin-driven electrolyte shifts of refeeding.
distractorExplanations.d: Energy restriction does not cause refeeding syndrome; the risk comes from rapidly feeding a starved patient.

options.a: Broth, milk, strained cream soups, and pulp-free juices
options.b: Broth, gelatin, clear juices, tea/coffee without cream
options.c: Gelatin, pudding, nectar juices, and coffee with cream
options.d: Broth, ice cream, sherbet, and orange juice with pulp

distractorExplanations.a: Milk and strained cream soups are full liquids; a clear liquid diet excludes dairy and opaque items.
distractorExplanations.c: Pudding, nectars, and cream are full-liquid items; only the gelatin belongs on a clear liquid diet.
distractorExplanations.d: Ice cream, sherbet, and juice with pulp are full liquids; a clear liquid diet uses transparent, pulp-free fluids.

options.a: Liberal sodium to offset diuretic losses, with fluids taken freely
options.b: Potassium restriction for every patient taking a loop diuretic
options.c: Sodium restriction individualized and fluid management as indicated
options.d: Fluid loading with 3–4 L/day to protect renal perfusion on diuretics

distractorExplanations.a: Liberal sodium and free fluids worsen congestion; heart failure MNT limits sodium and manages fluid as indicated.
distractorExplanations.b: Loop diuretics waste potassium, so these patients more often need potassium repletion, not routine restriction.
distractorExplanations.d: Large fluid intakes worsen volume overload; fluid restriction (often 1.5–2 L/day) is used when congestion persists.

options.a: Serum albumin, prealbumin, and CRP trends drawn during the same visit
options.b: Temporal wasting, orbital fat pads, muscle at clavicle/shoulder, edema
options.c: Diet history, 24-hour recall, and food frequency questionnaire results
options.d: Weight history, BMI, and percent usual body weight from the chart

distractorExplanations.a: These are biochemical data, a separate assessment domain; NFPE is a hands-on physical exam of fat, muscle, and fluid.
distractorExplanations.c: These are food/nutrition-related history methods; they assess intake, not physical signs found on examination.
distractorExplanations.d: These are anthropometric measurements, a separate domain; NFPE inspects and palpates for fat and muscle loss and edema.

options.a: Three larger meals, liquids taken with food, and fruit juice for energy
options.b: Small frequent meals, limit simple sugars, separate liquids from solids
options.c: Small frequent meals, high simple sugars, and fluids with each bite
options.d: Clear liquids for 48 hours, then a low-fat, low-fiber full liquid diet

distractorExplanations.a: Large meals, fluids with food, and juice speed gastric emptying and add osmotic load, worsening dumping symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: Meal size is right, but simple sugars and fluids with meals increase osmotic load and rapid transit into the jejunum.
distractorExplanations.d: Liquid diets empty fastest and full liquids are often high in sugar, so this would aggravate dumping syndrome.

options.a: Heat released by the body inside a sealed chamber
options.b: Oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production
options.c: Urinary nitrogen excretion over 24 hours
options.d: Body weight, height, age, and sex in a prediction equation

distractorExplanations.a: Measuring heat output in a chamber is direct calorimetry; indirect calorimetry uses respiratory gas exchange.
distractorExplanations.c: 24-hour urinary urea nitrogen estimates protein catabolism and nitrogen balance, not total energy expenditure.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes predictive equations such as Mifflin-St Jeor, which estimate rather than measure energy expenditure.

options.a: Routine high-dose zinc and vitamin C for every patient without deficiency
options.b: Energy restriction to promote weight loss before the wound can close
options.c: Fluid restriction to reduce edema around the wound bed
options.d: Adequate energy and protein, correct deficiencies, manage hydration

distractorExplanations.a: Guidelines support supplementing zinc or vitamin C when deficiency is suspected, not routine high doses for all.
distractorExplanations.b: Wound healing raises energy needs (about 30–35 kcal/kg); restriction slows healing and promotes protein loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Adequate hydration supports tissue perfusion; wound guidelines call for about 1 mL fluid/kcal unless contraindicated.

options.a: Inspecting finished products for defects before they reach customers
options.b: Documenting sanitation schedules for floors, walls, and equipment
options.c: Tracking food and labor costs at each step of production
options.d: Identifying critical control points to prevent food safety hazards

distractorExplanations.a: End-product inspection is reactive quality control; HACCP prevents hazards by controlling steps during production.
distractorExplanations.b: Cleaning schedules are prerequisite programs (SSOPs) that support HACCP but are not the CCP-based plan itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Cost tracking is a financial control; HACCP addresses biological, chemical, and physical hazards, not costs.

options.a: First in, first out — older stock used first
options.b: Last in, first out — newest stock used first
options.c: First expired, first out — stock used by expiration date
options.d: Fixed inventory, fixed order — stock reordered at par

distractorExplanations.b: That is LIFO, which uses the newest stock first and lets older product expire; FIFO rotates the oldest stock out first.
distractorExplanations.c: That is FEFO, a related rotation method keyed to expiration dates; FIFO is keyed to the date product was received.
distractorExplanations.d: Reordering to a par level is a purchasing method, not a stock rotation rule, and is not what the FIFO acronym means.

options.a: Allows cooks to adjust ingredients freely to suit each day's taste
options.b: Eliminates the need for production forecasting and receiving checks
options.c: Ensures consistent yield, quality, cost, and nutrient content
options.d: Sets the purchase specifications that vendors must meet on delivery

distractorExplanations.a: Free adjustment defeats standardization; a standardized recipe fixes ingredients and method to keep results consistent.
distractorExplanations.b: Forecasting and receiving are separate controls; standardized recipes support them but do not replace either one.
distractorExplanations.d: Purchase specifications describe the product vendors deliver; a standardized recipe governs how it is produced.

options.a: Cooking, rapid freezing, frozen storage for months, then thawing for service
options.b: Cooking, hot holding at 135°F or above until service later that day
options.c: Purchasing prepared foods, cold storage, then heating for service
options.d: Cooking, rapid chilling, refrigerated storage, then rethermalization for service

distractorExplanations.a: That describes cook-freeze, a sibling ready-prepared system; cook-chill stores food refrigerated, not frozen.
distractorExplanations.b: Cooking then hot holding for same-day service is conventional production, with no chilling or rethermalization step.
distractorExplanations.c: Heating purchased prepared foods is assembly-serve; in cook-chill the operation cooks the food itself before chilling.

options.a: Cooking to a safe internal temperature (eg, 165°F) verified by thermometer
options.b: Receiving poultry at 50°F or below, verified by a delivery thermometer
options.c: Cooking to an internal temperature of 145°F held for 15 seconds
options.d: Washing raw poultry in the sink before cooking to remove pathogens

distractorExplanations.b: Cold TCS food must be received at 41°F or below; 50°F is in the danger zone and is not a valid critical limit.
distractorExplanations.c: 145°F for 15 seconds is the Food Code limit for whole-muscle meats and fish; poultry requires 165°F.
distractorExplanations.d: Washing raw poultry spreads pathogens by splashing and does not eliminate them, so it cannot serve as a CCP.

options.a: (Food sales revenue / cost of food used) × 100
options.b: (Cost of food purchased / total operating cost) × 100
options.c: (Cost of food used / number of meals served) × 100
options.d: (Cost of food used / foodsales revenue) × 100

distractorExplanations.a: Inverts the ratio; food cost percentage puts cost of food used in the numerator and food sales in the denominator.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses purchases instead of food used and total operating cost instead of sales, so it is not food cost percentage.
distractorExplanations.c: Dividing food cost by meals gives cost per meal, a dollar figure; multiplying it by 100 does not make a sales percentage.

options.a: Planning a new single-use menu each week to maximize seasonal variety
options.b: Offering one unchanging menu daily so production sheets stay the same
options.c: Letting each cook choose dishes daily from available inventory, leftovers, and specials
options.d: Repeating a planned set of menus over a period to streamline purchasing and production

distractorExplanations.a: Single-use menus are written once and not repeated; a cycle menu's benefit comes from repeating planned menus.
distractorExplanations.b: One unchanging daily menu is a static menu, typical of restaurants; a cycle menu rotates several different days.
distractorExplanations.c: Daily cook choice from inventory resembles a market menu and loses the forecasting benefits a cycle menu provides.

options.a: Ice-point method, adjusting the dial to read 41°F
options.b: Room-temperature water compared with a wall thermostat
options.c: Ice-point (32°F) and/or boiling-point methods
options.d: Boiling-point method set to read 212°F at any altitude

distractorExplanations.a: 41°F is the cold-holding limit; in an ice-point check the thermometer is adjusted to read 32°F (0°C).
distractorExplanations.b: Room-temperature water and a wall thermostat give no fixed reference point, so they cannot verify accuracy.
distractorExplanations.d: Water boils below 212°F at higher altitudes, so the boiling-point reference must be adjusted for elevation.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-010.explanation: Calibrating food thermometers using ice-point (32°F / 0°C) and/or boiling-point (212°F / 100°C at sea level) methods ensures their accuracy. Regular calibration is crucial for monitoring critical control points and maintaining food safety. Choose the method that fits the thermometer and the range it will be used for.

options.a: Increase calorie density for patients with poor appetite
options.b: Match food/drink textures to swallowing safety needs
options.c: Standardize portion sizes for patients on calorie-controlled diets
options.d: Replace the clinical swallow evaluation by a speech-language pathologist

distractorExplanations.a: Calorie fortification addresses intake, not swallowing; IDDSI levels describe texture and flow for dysphagia safety.
distractorExplanations.c: Portion control is a calorie-management tool; IDDSI is a framework for food and drink texture, not portion size.
distractorExplanations.d: The SLP evaluation determines which IDDSI level is safe; texture-modified diets implement it, not replace it.

options.a: Accepting if ≤45°F with intact packaging, since trucks warm during unloading
options.b: Accepting if ≤50°F when the product will be cooked within 4 hours
options.c: Accepting if ≤41°F (or per code) with intact packaging and proper dating
options.d: Accepting if ≤41°F even if packages are torn, provided the product is cooked

distractorExplanations.a: The general receiving limit for cold TCS food is 41°F; the 45°F allowance applies only to specific items like milk.
distractorExplanations.b: 50°F is in the danger zone; planned cooking does not justify accepting temperature-abused TCS food.
distractorExplanations.d: Temperature is right, but torn packaging is a reason to reject; cooking does not correct possible contamination.

options.a: Verify cooking temperatures at critical control points
options.b: Calculate staff productivity in meals per labor hour
options.c: Evaluate acceptance and adjust menus/portions
options.d: Audit sanitizer concentration in dish machines

distractorExplanations.a: CCP temperatures are verified with thermometers and logs; plate waste measures how much served food is eaten.
distractorExplanations.b: Meals per labor hour relates output to staffing hours; plate waste data say nothing about labor productivity.
distractorExplanations.d: Sanitizer concentration is checked with test strips; plate waste studies assess food acceptance and portioning.

options.a: Nontyphoidal Salmonella (e.g., Typhimurium)
options.b: Shiga toxin–producing E. coli (e.g., O157:H7)
options.c: Clostridium perfringens (e.g., type A)
options.d: Listeria monocytogenes (e.g., serotype 4b)

distractorExplanations.a: Salmonella causes gastroenteritis linked to poultry and eggs but does not produce Shiga toxin or cause classic HUS.
distractorExplanations.c: C. perfringens causes illness from cooked meats cooled or held improperly, not HUS from undercooked ground beef.
distractorExplanations.d: Listeria is linked to ready-to-eat deli meats and soft cheeses and causes listeriosis, not Shiga toxin–driven HUS.

options.a: Maintain quality and reduce holding time in the danger zone
options.b: Reduce labor by preparing the full day's volume in one session
options.c: Lower food cost by using larger, discounted bulk ingredient packs
options.d: Eliminate the need for hot-holding temperature checks during service

distractorExplanations.b: Cooking the full volume at once is the opposite of batch cooking, which staggers small batches through service.
distractorExplanations.c: Batch cooking is about timing production to service, not purchasing; ingredient pack size is a buying decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Held food must still be monitored; batch cooking shortens holding time but does not remove temperature checks.

options.a: Lists step-by-step tasks; procedures state the broad rules behind them
options.b: States guiding principles/rules; procedures detail how to carry them out
options.c: Applies to one shift only; procedures apply across the organization
options.d: Defines a single position's duties and required qualifications

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the two: procedures give the step-by-step method, while policies state the guiding rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Policies are broad, organization-wide guides; scope by shift is not what distinguishes a policy from a procedure.
distractorExplanations.d: Duties and qualifications for one position make up a job description, not a policy.

options.a: Number of management levels between frontline staff and the CEO
options.b: Range of decisions a manager may make without higher approval
options.c: Number of employees a manager directly supervises effectively
options.d: Principle that each employee reports to only one supervisor

distractorExplanations.a: Levels of management describe organizational height (tall vs flat); span of control counts direct reports per manager.
distractorExplanations.b: Decision latitude describes delegated authority, not the number of employees a manager supervises.
distractorExplanations.d: One employee reporting to one supervisor is unity of command, a different organizing principle.

options.a: The supervisor's overall impression from the most recent month
options.b: Comparison with coworkers' ratings to fit a forced distribution
options.c: Documented job-related standards and observed performance
options.d: Employee self-assessment, accepted as the final rating

distractorExplanations.a: Rating on recent impressions is the recency error; appraisals should cover the full period against set standards.
distractorExplanations.b: Forced distribution ranks people against each other rather than against documented job standards.
distractorExplanations.d: Self-assessment can inform the discussion, but the appraisal must rest on the supervisor's documented observations.

options.a: Recurring food, supply, and labor costs for the fiscal year
options.b: Projected cash receipts and payments for each month of the year
options.c: Major equipment and facility investments with multi-year value
options.d: Small wares such as pans and utensils replaced as they wear out

distractorExplanations.a: Recurring food, supply, and labor costs are planned in the operating budget, not the capital budget.
distractorExplanations.b: Monthly receipts and payments are planned in the cash budget, which tracks liquidity rather than long-term assets.
distractorExplanations.d: Small wares fall below capital cost thresholds and are expensed through the operating budget.

options.a: Measures whether a program's objectives were achieved after implementation
options.b: Tracks how many sessions were delivered and who attended them
options.c: Identifies health/nutrition problems, resources, and priorities in a population
options.d: Identifies one patient's nutrition diagnosis using a PES statement

distractorExplanations.a: That is outcome evaluation, done after a program runs; a needs assessment comes first to identify problems.
distractorExplanations.b: Counting sessions and attendance is process evaluation of a running program, not a pre-planning needs assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: A PES statement documents one patient's nutrition diagnosis in the NCP; needs assessment looks at a population.

options.a: Sales orientation that pushes volume through aggressive promotion
options.b: Relationship/marketing orientation beyond one-time sales
options.c: Production orientation focused on efficient, low-cost output
options.d: Product orientation focused on quality features over customer needs

distractorExplanations.a: A sales orientation stresses persuading customers to buy now, focusing on transactions rather than lasting relationships.
distractorExplanations.c: A production orientation assumes customers want cheap, available products and centers on efficiency, not relationships.
distractorExplanations.d: A product orientation assumes quality alone sells and can ignore what customers want, unlike relationship marketing.

options.a: Employment decisions based on protected classes such as race, sex, religion
options.b: Hiring based on bona fide occupational qualifications tied to the job
options.c: Requiring a valid food handler card as a condition of employment
options.d: Posting job requirements tied to essential functions of the position

distractorExplanations.b: BFOQs are a recognized legal exception; EEO law permits job-related qualifications that are genuinely necessary.
distractorExplanations.c: A job-related credential required by food code applies to every applicant equally, so EEO does not prohibit it.
distractorExplanations.d: Defining essential functions is lawful and supports ADA reasonable accommodation decisions; EEO does not bar it.

rd-exam-readiness-check-management-011.explanation: Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) principles prohibit discrimination in employment decisions based on protected characteristics such as race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, disability, or genetic information. These laws aim to ensure fair treatment for all applicants and employees. Protected classes are defined by law (Title VII, ADEA, ADA, and related statutes).

options.a: Map an organization's reporting lines
options.b: Show the frequency of defect causes
options.c: Schedule project tasks over time
options.d: Map steps of a process with decision points

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting lines are shown on an organizational chart; a Gantt chart plots tasks against a timeline.
distractorExplanations.b: Ranking how often causes occur is a Pareto chart, a quality tool, not a project scheduling tool.
distractorExplanations.d: Process steps with decision points are drawn as a flowchart; a Gantt chart shows task durations over time.

options.a: Monthly benefits for low-income households to buy groceries at retailers
options.b: Nutrition education and supplemental foods for eligible women, infants, and children
options.c: Free or reduced-price breakfasts and lunches for eligible children in participating schools
options.d: Congregate and home-delivered meals for eligible adults aged 60 and older

distractorExplanations.a: That describes SNAP, which gives general grocery benefits to households; WIC targets pregnant/postpartum women and children under 5.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes the National School Lunch Program; WIC serves infants and children up to age 5, not school meals.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes Older Americans Act nutrition programs; WIC serves women, infants, and young children.

options.a: How many sessions, flyers, and contacts the program delivered
options.b: Whether the program was implemented as planned and reached the target group
options.c: Health problems, resources, and priorities before the program begins
options.d: Whether objectives/changes in knowledge, behavior, or health status were achieved

distractorExplanations.a: Counts of sessions and materials are process or output measures; outcome evaluation looks at participant change.
distractorExplanations.b: Fidelity and reach are assessed in process evaluation; outcome evaluation asks whether objectives were met.
distractorExplanations.c: Identifying problems and resources before launch is a needs assessment, the planning step, not outcome evaluation.

options.a: 50% of healthy individuals in a specific life-stage and gender group
options.b: 97–98% of healthy individuals in a specific life-stage and gender group
options.c: Most healthy individuals, based on observed intakes when data are limited
options.d: Nearly every individual without risk of adverse effects from excess intake

distractorExplanations.b: Covering 97–98% of the group defines the RDA, which is set about two standard deviations above the EAR.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes the Adequate Intake (AI), used when evidence is too limited to establish an EAR.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL), which concerns excess intake, not the median requirement.

options.a: Vitamins A, D, E, and K
options.b: Vitamin C and B-complex vitamins
options.c: Vitamin C, folate, and vitamin E
options.d: B-complex vitamins and vitamin K

distractorExplanations.c: Vitamin C and folate are water-soluble, but vitamin E is fat-soluble, so this set mixes the two classes.
distractorExplanations.d: The B vitamins are water-soluble, but vitamin K is fat-soluble and absorbed with dietary fat in micelles.
distractorExplanations.a: A, D, E, K are fat-soluble.

options.a: Endogenous triglycerides synthesized in the liver
options.b: Cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver
options.c: Dietary (exogenous) triglycerides from the intestine
options.d: Cholesterol from the liver to peripheral tissues

distractorExplanations.a: Liver-made (endogenous) triglycerides are packaged in VLDL; chylomicrons carry dietary fat from the gut.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverse cholesterol transport from tissues to the liver is the role of HDL, not chylomicrons.
distractorExplanations.d: Delivering cholesterol from the liver to tissues is the role of LDL, derived from VLDL, not chylomicrons.

options.a: Elevated waist circumference, blood pressure, triglycerides, fasting glucose, and low HDL
options.b: Elevated body mass index, LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, HbA1c, and C-reactive protein
options.c: Elevated waist circumference, LDL cholesterol, uric acid, and fasting insulin
options.d: Elevated body weight, total cholesterol, HbA1c, and low serum albumin

distractorExplanations.b: BMI, LDL, total cholesterol, HbA1c, and CRP are not among the five NCEP ATP III/IDF metabolic syndrome criteria.
distractorExplanations.c: Waist circumference counts, but LDL, uric acid, and fasting insulin are not metabolic syndrome criteria.
distractorExplanations.d: Body weight, total cholesterol, HbA1c, and albumin are not criteria; low HDL and high triglycerides are used instead.

rd-exam-readiness-check-principles-025.explanation: Metabolic syndrome clusters cardiometabolic risk factors including central adiposity and dyslipidemia. Criteria sets include NCEP ATP III and the IDF/AHA harmonized definition.

options.a: Carbonic anhydrase
options.b: Glutathione peroxidase
options.c: Superoxide dismutase
options.d: Cytochrome c oxidase

distractorExplanations.c: Superoxide dismutase is an antioxidant enzyme, but it uses copper/zinc or manganese, not selenium.
distractorExplanations.d: Cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport chain is a copper- and iron-containing enzyme, not selenium.
distractorExplanations.a: Carbonic anhydrase uses zinc.

options.a: Is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen
options.b: Activates clotting factors through gamma-carboxylation of glutamate
options.c: Supports protein synthesis, cell proliferation, and immune function
options.d: Forms the core of hemoglobin that carries oxygen to the wound bed

distractorExplanations.a: Proline and lysine hydroxylation for collagen requires vitamin C; zinc acts in protein synthesis and cell division.
distractorExplanations.b: Gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors is the role of vitamin K, not zinc.
distractorExplanations.d: Iron, not zinc, sits at the center of the heme in hemoglobin and carries oxygen.

options.a: Reduced lung cancer incidence in intervention trials
options.b: Increased lung cancer risk in intervention trials
options.c: Vitamin A toxicity from excess conversion to retinol
options.d: Reduced cardiovascular mortality in intervention trials

distractorExplanations.a: ATBC and CARET found more lung cancer, not less, in smokers given beta-carotene, so CARET was stopped early.
distractorExplanations.c: Conversion of beta-carotene to retinol is regulated, so supplements do not cause vitamin A toxicity.
distractorExplanations.d: These trials showed no cardiovascular benefit; ATBC and CARET reported equal or higher total mortality.

options.a: Inadequate oral intake related to 8% weight loss in 3 months as evidenced by poor appetite
options.b: Unintended weight loss related to colon cancer as evidenced by patient report of feeling tired
options.c: Unintended weight loss related to 8% loss in 3 months as evidenced by inadequate intake
options.d: Unintended weight loss related to inadequate oral intake as evidenced by 8% loss in 3 months

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the sign (weight loss) as the etiology; the etiology should be the cause, with measured loss as the evidence.
distractorExplanations.b: Fatigue does not measure weight loss, and the medical diagnosis alone is not an etiology the RD can address.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps etiology and signs: the 8% loss is the evidence, and inadequate intake is the cause.

options.a: Match prandial insulin doses to planned carbohydrate intake
options.b: Set a fixed daily carbohydrate limit that replaces insulin titration
options.c: Match basal insulin doses to the day's total protein intake
options.d: Rank foods by glycemic index so high-GI foods can be dropped

distractorExplanations.b: Carbohydrate counting is used to adjust insulin, not to replace titration with a fixed carbohydrate cap.
distractorExplanations.c: Basal insulin covers fasting needs; bolus (prandial) insulin is matched to carbohydrate, not protein.
distractorExplanations.d: Ranking foods by GI is a different tool; carbohydrate counting quantifies grams to dose mealtime insulin.

options.a: Cottage cheese, scrambled eggs, and mashed potatoes
options.b: Milk, strained cream soups, and pudding
options.c: Milk, cream soups with noodles, and rice pudding
options.d: Pureed meats, mashed bananas, and applesauce

distractorExplanations.a: These are soft-diet solids; a full liquid diet is limited to foods that are liquid or pourable at body temperature.
distractorExplanations.c: Milk is allowed, but noodles and rice add solid pieces, which are excluded on a full liquid diet.
distractorExplanations.d: Pureed meats and fruits belong to a pureed (IDDSI level 4) diet, not a full liquid diet.

rd-exam-readiness-check-nutrition-care-0.explanation: Full liquids are pourable at room temperature and may include milk-based items per order. Items are given per the physician's diet order.

options.a: Avoiding leafy green vegetables so the INR stays within the target range
options.b: Increasing vitamin K foods on days a warfarin dose is missed to keep INR steady
options.c: Consistent vitamin K intake rather than eliminating all vitamin K foods
options.d: Taking vitamin K supplements with each warfarin dose

distractorExplanations.a: Avoiding greens makes intake erratic and harms diet quality; warfarin doses are set around a steady vitamin K intake.
distractorExplanations.b: Extra vitamin K on a missed-dose day further lowers INR; a missed dose is handled per prescriber instructions.
distractorExplanations.d: Vitamin K supplements counteract warfarin; low-dose vitamin K is only given by prescribers for specific INR goals.

options.a: Increase fluid intake because thick liquids improve hydration
options.b: Speed oral transit so the swallow is triggered sooner
options.c: Raise calorie density for patients with poor oral intake
options.d: Slow bolus flow and reduce aspiration into the airway

distractorExplanations.a: Thickened liquids are often less palatable and can reduce fluid intake, so hydration must be monitored closely.
distractorExplanations.b: Thickening slows bolus flow to give more time for airway closure; faster transit would raise aspiration risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Most thickeners add little energy; the purpose is safer bolus control, not calorie fortification.

options.a: Sodium restriction and adequate protein
options.b: Low-fat diet and limited animal protein
options.c: Liberal sodium with fluid restriction to 1 L
options.d: Sodium restriction and 0.5 g/kg protein

distractorExplanations.b: Fat restriction is not indicated, and limiting protein worsens sarcopenia; cirrhosis needs about 1.2–1.5 g/kg.
distractorExplanations.c: Sodium drives ascites, so it is restricted (about 2 g/day); fluid restriction is reserved for severe hyponatremia.
distractorExplanations.d: Sodium restriction is right, but 0.5 g/kg protein is outdated and promotes muscle loss; adequate protein is advised.

rd-exam-readiness-check-nutrition-care-0.explanation: Ascites management limits sodium; protein is usually adequate unless encephalopathy dictates change. Protein is modified only if hepatic encephalopathy requires it.

options.a: Increased to 1.2 g/kg/day to offset protein losses as GFR declines
options.b: Moderately restricted while maintaining adequate calories and quality protein
options.c: Restricted to 0.6 g/kg/day with energy cut to promote weight loss
options.d: Unrestricted protein, with phosphorus binders used to offset the extra protein load

distractorExplanations.a: About 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day is the target once on dialysis; non-dialysis CKD 3–4 uses moderate protein restriction.
distractorExplanations.c: The protein level is in range, but energy must stay adequate (about 25–35 kcal/kg) to prevent protein wasting.
distractorExplanations.d: Phosphate binders control phosphorus, not protein load; unrestricted protein may speed CKD progression.

options.a: High-sodium foods such as canned soups, deli meats, and pickles
options.b: High-phosphorus foods such as colas, processed cheese, and nuts
options.c: High-potassium foods such as bananas, oranges, and salt substitutes
options.d: Refined grains such as white rice, white bread, and plain pasta

distractorExplanations.a: Sodium restriction targets blood pressure and fluid; it does not lower serum potassium in hyperkalemia.
distractorExplanations.b: Phosphorus restriction treats hyperphosphatemia; it is a separate CKD electrolyte goal from potassium.
distractorExplanations.d: Refined grains are low in potassium and are often recommended in place of whole grains on a low-K diet.

rd-exam-readiness-check-nutrition-care-0.explanation: Potassium restriction targets concentrated sources and KCl salt substitutes when hyperkalemia is present. Salt substitutes are a hidden source because they contain potassium chloride.

options.a: Sodium, chloride, albumin, and prealbumin levels
options.b: Calcium, vitamin D, zinc, and serum ferritin
options.c: Total cholesterol, triglycerides, and HbA1c
options.d: Phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, and thiamin status

distractorExplanations.a: Albumin and prealbumin reflect inflammation, and sodium/chloride are not the hallmark intracellular shifts of refeeding.
distractorExplanations.b: These markers relate to bone and micronutrient status; refeeding causes acute drops in phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium.
distractorExplanations.c: Lipids and HbA1c change over weeks to months and do not detect the acute electrolyte shifts of refeeding.

options.a: NPO status with transition to enteral feeding when clinically appropriate
options.b: Routine parenteral nutrition from day one to rest the pancreas
options.c: Clear liquids by mouth for 7 days before any enteral tube feeding is considered
options.d: High-fat oral supplements to meet energy needs quickly

distractorExplanations.b: Enteral is preferred over parenteral nutrition; PN is reserved for patients who cannot meet needs enterally.
distractorExplanations.c: Delaying nutrition for a week raises infection and malnutrition risk; enteral feeding should start early if tolerated.
distractorExplanations.d: Oral intake is not tolerated in this case, and high-fat feeds stimulate pancreatic secretion and pain.

options.a: Non-heme iron sources taken with black tea at meals to enhance absorption
options.b: Heme and non-heme iron sources with vitamin C to enhance absorption
options.c: Non-heme iron sources taken with milk to enhance absorption
options.d: Heme iron sources taken with a calcium supplement at meals

distractorExplanations.a: Tea polyphenols (tannins) inhibit non-heme iron absorption; tea should be taken between meals instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Calcium in milk inhibits iron absorption, so milk is a poor pairing with iron-rich meals.
distractorExplanations.d: Calcium supplements reduce both heme and non-heme iron absorption when taken with an iron-rich meal.

options.a: Regular milk in large servings to build up lactase activity
options.b: Evaporated milk, which has less lactose than fluid milk
options.c: Lactose-free milk or yogurt with live cultures in small portions
options.d: Calcium-fortified goat milk, which is naturally lactose-free

distractorExplanations.a: Large servings of regular milk cause symptoms; tolerance improves with small amounts spread through the day.
distractorExplanations.b: Evaporated milk is concentrated, so it has about twice the lactose of fluid milk per cup.
distractorExplanations.d: Goat milk contains lactose (about 4%) in amounts similar to cow's milk, so it is not lactose-free.

options.a: Strict restriction of tyrosine, with a medical formula supplying extra phenylalanine instead
options.b: Restriction of leucine, isoleucine, and valine with a BCAA-free formula
options.c: Restriction of galactose and lactose with a soy-based infant formula
options.d: Strict restriction of phenylalanine with medical formula providing other amino acids

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses PKU therapy: phenylalanine is restricted, and tyrosine becomes conditionally essential and is supplied.
distractorExplanations.b: Restricting branched-chain amino acids treats maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), not PKU.
distractorExplanations.c: Galactose and lactose restriction treats galactosemia; PKU restricts the amino acid phenylalanine.

options.a: Small frequent meals, lower fat and fiber, and texture modification
options.b: Three large meals, higher fiber, and lying down after eating
options.c: Small frequent meals, high fiber, and raw vegetables for motility
options.d: Three large meals with high-fat foods to slow nutrient delivery

distractorExplanations.b: Large meals and fiber slow emptying further, and lying down after eating also delays gastric emptying.
distractorExplanations.c: Meal size is right, but high fiber and raw vegetables delay emptying and can form bezoars in gastroparesis.
distractorExplanations.d: Large, high-fat meals delay gastric emptying, which is already impaired in gastroparesis.

rd-exam-readiness-check-nutrition-care-0.explanation: Reduced gastric emptying responds to smaller, lower-residue meals and individualized fluid timing. Texture modification (e.g., more liquid or pureed foods) is advanced as tolerated.

options.a: Starting at 3,000 kcal/day to reverse weight loss quickly
options.b: Gradual calorie advancement with electrolyte and cardiac monitoring
options.c: High-protein, very-low-carbohydrate meals to limit insulin surges
options.d: Weight gain targets of 3–4 kg per week from the first week

distractorExplanations.a: Starting high without monitoring risks refeeding syndrome; energy is advanced gradually with electrolyte checks.
distractorExplanations.c: Carbohydrate is needed for recovery and is not eliminated; refeeding risk is managed with gradual energy increases and electrolyte checks.
distractorExplanations.d: Typical inpatient targets are about 0.5–1.5 kg per week; 3–4 kg per week is unsafe and mostly fluid.

options.a: Identify critical control points in the flow of food
options.b: Establish critical limits for each control point
options.c: Establish monitoring procedures for each control point
options.d: Conduct a hazard analysis of ingredients and processes

distractorExplanations.a: Identifying CCPs is HACCP principle 2; it depends on the hazard analysis completed in principle 1.
distractorExplanations.b: Setting critical limits is principle 3; limits cannot be set until hazards and CCPs are identified.
distractorExplanations.c: Monitoring procedures are principle 4, which comes after hazard analysis, CCPs, and critical limits.

options.a: A probe thermometer reading of the sanitizer water
options.b: Visual color of the solution compared with fresh water
options.c: Test strips or titration per manufacturer instructions
options.d: A pH strip confirming the solution is acidic

distractorExplanations.a: Water temperature affects sanitizer efficacy but does not measure concentration in ppm.
distractorExplanations.b: Color does not indicate concentration; sanitizer strength is verified with a test kit matched to the chemical.
distractorExplanations.d: pH influences how well sanitizers work but does not measure ppm; concentration needs a test strip or titration.

options.a: The lowest bid price on each purchase order for the contract period
options.b: Delivery on the same day the order is placed
options.c: Exemption from temperature and quality checks on delivered goods
options.d: Products meet inspection, traceability, and safety standards

distractorExplanations.a: Approved-source rules are about food safety and inspection; bid price is a separate purchasing decision.
distractorExplanations.b: Delivery timing is a service term in the vendor contract, not what the approved-source requirement guarantees.
distractorExplanations.c: Deliveries from approved suppliers must still be inspected for temperature, packaging, and quality on receipt.

options.a: Correct practices after each health inspection
options.b: Rely on end-product testing to confirm safety
options.c: Take preventive actions and monitor CCPs
options.d: Delegate food safety oversight to the vendor

distractorExplanations.a: Fixing problems after inspections is reactive; active managerial control builds prevention into daily operations.
distractorExplanations.b: End-product testing detects problems after the fact; active control monitors CCPs during production.
distractorExplanations.d: The person in charge stays responsible for food safety; it cannot be handed to suppliers.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-023.explanation: Active control includes training, monitoring, and corrective action before outbreaks. Active managerial control is proactive rather than only reacting to violations.

options.a: Cooking ground beef to 155°F and holding hot foods at 135°F or above
options.b: Restricting ill employees to dishwashing duty and wiping surfaces with quaternary ammonium
options.c: Using hand sanitizer in place of handwashing and cleaning dining tables once daily
options.d: Excluding ill employees, enforcing hand hygiene, and sanitizing high-touch surfaces

distractorExplanations.a: These are time/temperature controls for bacteria in meat; norovirus spreads mainly through ill workers and surfaces.
distractorExplanations.b: Vomiting or diarrhea requires exclusion, not restriction, and quats work poorly on norovirus; chlorine is preferred.
distractorExplanations.c: Hand sanitizer is not effective against norovirus and cannot replace handwashing; daily cleaning is too infrequent.

options.a: Edible portion weight and cost per serving after trimming and cooking loss
options.b: The as-purchased price per pound quoted on the vendor invoice
options.c: The minimum internal cooking temperature for each chicken cut
options.d: The number of portions to order based on patient census and menu popularity data

distractorExplanations.b: The AP price is an input to the yield test; the test converts it to edible-portion cost after losses.
distractorExplanations.c: Cooking temperatures are food safety standards; a yield test measures weight lost to trimming and cooking.
distractorExplanations.d: Forecasting portions from census is production planning; a yield test measures usable weight per purchase unit.

options.a: Cooking items in a central kitchen, then transporting them to service sites
options.b: Purchasing fully prepared or convenience foods that are assembled and served
options.c: Purchasing raw ingredients and cooking them on site close to service
options.d: Cooking and rapidly chilling foods for storage, then reheating on site

distractorExplanations.a: Central cooking and transport describes a commissary system, which still involves full production.
distractorExplanations.c: Cooking from raw ingredients on site is conventional production, the opposite of assembly-serve.
distractorExplanations.d: Cooking then chilling for later reheating describes ready-prepared (cook-chill) production.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-026.explanation: Assembly-serve uses commercially prepared items assembled on site, minimizing production labor and cooking. There is little or no on-site cooking.

options.a: Scheduled pesticide spraying by kitchen staff throughout food prep areas
options.b: Bait stations placed on food prep tables to catch pests where they feed
options.c: Exclusion, monitoring traps, sanitation, and documented corrective actions
options.d: Calling a pest control operator only after droppings are found

distractorExplanations.a: IPM relies on prevention first; pesticides are applied by a licensed operator, not routinely by kitchen staff.
distractorExplanations.b: Bait and pesticides must be kept away from food-contact surfaces; placing them on prep tables risks contamination.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for droppings is reactive; IPM uses ongoing monitoring and prevention before an infestation is visible.

options.a: Vacuum seal integrity alone, since oxygen removal prevents growth
options.b: Final cooking temperature only, since chilling is optional after pasteurization
options.c: Product appearance and odor at rethermalization before service
options.d: Time–temperature pasteurization and rapid chilling records for each batch

distractorExplanations.a: Removing oxygen favors anaerobes such as C. botulinum, so time–temperature control is still essential.
distractorExplanations.b: Pasteurization leaves spores, so rapid chilling and cold holding must also be verified and recorded.
distractorExplanations.c: Sensory checks cannot detect pathogens or toxins; safety depends on documented time–temperature records.

options.a: Ready-to-eat refrigerated foods with extended shelf life
options.b: Low-acid canned foods that are improperly processed
options.c: Cooked rice held at room temperature after cooking
options.d: Raw shell eggs and undercooked poultry dishes

distractorExplanations.b: Improperly processed low-acid canned foods are the classic risk for Clostridium botulinum, not Listeria.
distractorExplanations.c: Cooked rice left at room temperature is the classic risk for Bacillus cereus, not Listeria.
distractorExplanations.d: Raw eggs and undercooked poultry are classic Salmonella (and Campylobacter) risks, not the RTE Listeria risk.

rd-exam-readiness-check-foodservice-029.explanation: L. monocytogenes grows at refrigeration temperatures in RTE products. Examples include deli meats, hot dogs, smoked seafood, and soft cheeses.

options.a: Hold cooked food at 135°F or above until service
options.b: Rapidly lower product temperature through the danger zone
options.c: Thaw frozen products quickly at room temperature
options.d: Store chilled food long term at 41°F or below until it is needed

distractorExplanations.a: Hot holding at 135°F or above is done with hot-holding equipment, not blast chillers designed for rapid cooling.
distractorExplanations.c: Room-temperature thawing is unsafe; blast chillers are for rapid cooling of cooked food, not thawing.
distractorExplanations.d: Long-term cold storage is done in walk-ins or reach-ins; blast chillers cool food quickly before storage.

options.a: The organization's desired future state in 5–10 years
options.b: Measurable targets the department must meet this quarter
options.c: The core beliefs that guide how staff behave
options.d: The organization's current purpose and whom it serves

distractorExplanations.a: A desired future state is the vision statement; the mission states the current purpose and whom it serves.
distractorExplanations.b: Measurable, time-bound targets are objectives that support the mission, not the mission statement itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Core beliefs guiding behavior are the organization's values statement, not its mission.

options.a: Authorization to provide medical nutrition therapy
options.b: Food safety knowledge for managers and food handlers
options.c: Eligibility to sit for the CDR registration exam
options.d: Exemption of the facility from routine health inspections

distractorExplanations.a: MNT is provided by RDNs under state licensure; a food safety certificate does not authorize clinical practice.
distractorExplanations.c: CDR exam eligibility requires an accredited degree and supervised practice, not a food safety certificate.
distractorExplanations.d: Certified managers are required by food code, but the facility is still inspected routinely.

options.a: Promise clients specific weight-loss results in writing
options.b: Share client records with family members on request
options.c: Provide competent, ethical, evidence-based nutrition care
options.d: Recommend supplements they sell to maximize client outcomes

distractorExplanations.a: The Code requires honesty about expected results; promising specific outcomes is misleading.
distractorExplanations.b: Disclosure needs client consent or legal authority; family requests alone do not override confidentiality.
distractorExplanations.d: Selling products to clients is a conflict of interest that must be disclosed and must not drive recommendations.

options.a: Payroll and benefits paperwork, with job training deferred for months
options.b: Advanced clinical MNT protocols for every new food service worker
options.c: A single video on company history, with skills learned on the job
options.d: Safety, sanitation, department policies, and job-specific training

distractorExplanations.a: Paperwork is part of onboarding, but delaying safety and job training leaves new staff unprepared to work safely.
distractorExplanations.b: Advanced MNT is outside a food service worker's role; orientation covers safety, sanitation, and job duties.
distractorExplanations.c: A history video omits required safety, sanitation, and policy content that orientation must cover.

options.a: Documented coaching, written warnings when needed, and clear expectations
options.b: Immediate termination for a first minor error to deter others
options.c: Verbal warnings only, with no written record to avoid conflict
options.d: Suspension without pay as the first step, followed by coaching if the problem repeats

distractorExplanations.b: Progressive discipline escalates step by step; termination is the final step, not the response to a first minor error.
distractorExplanations.c: Verbal warnings are the first step, but documentation is required to support fairness and later steps.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the sequence: coaching and verbal warnings come before suspension in progressive discipline.

options.a: Sales, workload, overhead, and turnover
options.b: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats
options.c: Strategies, weaknesses, objectives, and timelines
options.d: Staffing, wages, operations, and training

distractorExplanations.a: These are operating metrics; SWOT pairs internal strengths/weaknesses with external opportunities/threats.
distractorExplanations.c: Strategies and objectives come after a SWOT analysis; the S and O stand for strengths and opportunities.
distractorExplanations.d: These are internal operating areas; SWOT also scans external opportunities and threats.

options.a: Relates food cost to the number of meals served
options.b: Relates labor cost to total food sales revenue
options.c: Relates output (meals served) to staffing input
options.d: Relates patient satisfaction to staffing levels

distractorExplanations.a: Food cost divided by meals is food cost per meal, a cost metric, not a labor productivity measure.
distractorExplanations.b: Labor cost divided by sales is labor cost percentage; meals per labor hour uses meals and paid hours.
distractorExplanations.d: Satisfaction scores are quality measures; meals per labor hour relates meals produced to labor hours.

options.a: This year's budget to the prior year's budgeted amounts
options.b: Projected revenue to projected expenses before the period
options.c: Actual results to those of peer hospitals for a period
options.d: Actual financial results to budgeted amounts for a period

distractorExplanations.a: Comparing two budgets is trend analysis of plans; a variance report compares actual results with the budget.
distractorExplanations.b: Projecting revenue against expenses is budget preparation; variance analysis happens after actuals are known.
distractorExplanations.c: Comparing results with peer hospitals is benchmarking, not budget variance analysis.

options.a: Hand hygiene, excluding ill food handlers, and clean uniform protocols
options.b: Hand hygiene, gloves replacing handwashing, and clean uniform protocols
options.c: Hand sanitizer in place of handwashing and daily uniform checks
options.d: Bare-hand contact with ready-to-eat foods if hands were just washed

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves do not replace handwashing; hands must be washed before putting on gloves.
distractorExplanations.c: Hand sanitizer is not a substitute for handwashing in food handling, and this omits excluding ill workers.
distractorExplanations.d: Food Code prohibits bare-hand contact with ready-to-eat foods even after handwashing; utensils or gloves are required.

options.a: Sales minus cost of food sold, labor, and overhead for the period
options.b: Sales from food and beverage transactions before subtracting operating expenses
options.c: Sales minus the cost of food and beverages sold, before labor and overhead
options.d: Cash on hand at the end of the period after paying vendors

distractorExplanations.a: Subtracting food cost, labor, and overhead from sales gives net profit, not revenue.
distractorExplanations.c: Sales minus cost of goods sold is gross profit (contribution); revenue is total sales before any deduction.
distractorExplanations.d: End-of-period cash is a balance sheet figure; revenue is sales income earned during the period.

options.a: The clinic's mission and vision statements and logo design
options.b: Patient outcomes measured after the clinic's first year of operation
options.c: Market demand, projected costs, reimbursement, and staffing needs
options.d: Current inpatient census and cafeteria sales trends

distractorExplanations.a: Mission, vision, and branding come after deciding the clinic is viable; they do not test demand or finances.
distractorExplanations.b: First-year outcomes are measured by outcome evaluation after launch; feasibility is assessed before opening.
distractorExplanations.d: Inpatient census and café sales describe other services and do not show outpatient demand or reimbursement.

options.a: Menu pricing, café profitability, and retail sales growth
options.b: Patient satisfaction and taste-panel scores as the main accreditation measure
options.c: Staff union contracts and wage parity across departments
options.d: Patient safety, sanitation, and accurate therapeutic diet implementation

distractorExplanations.a: Retail financial performance is a management concern, not a Joint Commission accreditation standard.
distractorExplanations.b: Satisfaction data may support quality work, but standards focus on patient safety and correct diet delivery.
distractorExplanations.c: Labor contracts and wages fall under labor law and HR, not Joint Commission foodservice standards.

options.a: Identify performance gaps and adopt proven best practices
options.b: Set prices to match the lowest-cost peer hospital
options.c: Replace internal quality monitoring with peer hospitals' data
options.d: Prove compliance with state food code requirements

distractorExplanations.b: Benchmarking informs improvement; copying a peer's prices ignores local cost structure and goals.
distractorExplanations.c: Benchmarks add external context to internal monitoring; they do not replace ongoing QI data.
distractorExplanations.d: Food code compliance is shown through inspections; benchmarking compares performance metrics with peers.

options.a: Individual employees negotiating pay directly with managers
options.b: Negotiating wages, benefits, and working conditions
options.c: Filing a complaint with OSHA about workplace hazards
options.d: A state agency setting minimum wages for food workers

distractorExplanations.a: Individual negotiation is the opposite of collective bargaining, where the union bargains for the whole unit.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA complaints are a regulatory safety process, not negotiation of a labor contract with management.
distractorExplanations.d: Minimum wages are set by law; collective bargaining sets contract terms between management and the union.

rd-exam-readiness-check-management-030.explanation: Labor contracts are negotiated collectively per labor law and union agreements. Bargaining takes place between management and union representatives.
